case_context.legal_issue: Whether the proscription orders infringed the petitioner's fundamental right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the proscription of the J.V.P. prevented members from assembling peacefully as a political party, infringing Article 14(1)(b).
case_context.respondent_argument: The Attorney-General contended that the President's immunity under Article 35(1) barred proceedings and that the proscription was lawful under Emergency Regulations, not subject to challenge against the Attorney-General.
key_facts: J.V.P. was proscribed by the President under Emergency Regulations.
The petitioner and members were prevented from functioning as a political party and assembling.
The petitioner alleged mala fide motives behind the proscription.
The petitioner cited infringement of Article 14(1)(b) rights.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court acknowledged the right to peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b) but emphasized the procedural barrier posed by the President's immunity under Article 35(1). Since the proscription was under Emergency Regulations and not under powers assigned under Article 44(2), the Attorney-General was not the proper respondent and the petition was not maintainable.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The proscription order prevented peaceful assembly by proscribing the party, but the court held that the immunity and procedural rules prevented adjudication on this claim in the present petition.
principles_established: Absolute immunity of the President under Article 35(1) applies to acts not under Article 44(2).
Proceedings against the President for acts under Article 44(2) must be against the Attorney-General.
Proscription under Emergency Regulations is not an act under Article 44(2).

outcome.holding: The petition alleging infringement of Article 14(1)(b) rights was dismissed for lack of proper party and jurisdiction.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(b) was a key part of the petitioner's fundamental rights claim regarding the proscription's effect on peaceful assembly, but the court's immunity and procedural ruling prevented relief.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner claimed infringement of freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b) due to proscription; the court held the Attorney-General was not the proper respondent and dismissed the petition.
